column1: What three invariants enable Unreal's UObject system to provide memory safety in native C++?
column2: 1) All engine-managed objects derive from UObject and live in engine-tracked heap allocations, 2) object lifetime is governed by an incremental mark-and-sweep GC using reachability from a root set, 3) raw C++ pointers between objects are tracked via a write barrier system that notifies the collector of topology changes.

column1: Why does Unreal use a custom reflection system instead of native C++ RTTI?
column2: C++ lacks runtime introspection, automatic memory management, and stable cross-module ABI; Unreal's reflection system transforms annotated C++ declarations into queryable compile-time metadata to drive serialization, replication, GC, and editor/blueprint exposure from a single source of truth.

column1: What is the core architectural invariant of deferred rendering in Unreal Engine?
column2: Every pixel is shaded exactly once per light source regardless of overdraw, because geometric/material data is first written to the G-Buffer and lighting is computed in a separate screen-space pass decoupled from geometry complexity.

column1: What render targets typically compose Unreal's G-Buffer, and what do they encode?
column2: Five to seven full-resolution targets: octahedron-mapped world-space normals (16-bit float), base color + ambient occlusion (with alpha for metadata), and metallic/roughness/specular values used by the GGX microfacet BRDF.

column1: When Destroy() is called on an AActor, what actually happens immediately?
column2: No memory is freed. The actor's IsPendingKill flag is set true, it's removed from the tick list, its components are detached from the scene, and it's queued for removal from the ULevel. Actual deallocation happens later during a GC pass.

column1: Why should external references to actors you don't own use TWeakObjectPtr<T> instead of raw AActor*?
column2: Because Destroy() doesn't immediately deallocate memory—a raw pointer can become a dangling reference to memory that's still mapped but semantically dead; TWeakObjectPtr safely resolves to null when the object is pending kill or collected.

column1: How does the Blueprint Virtual Machine execute asynchronous, multi-frame operations without threading?
column2: Via latent actions: a continuation-passing mechanism where suspended execution contexts persist as heap-allocated state machines across frames, resuming when their completion predicates become true, all on the single gameplay thread.

column1: Approximately how much slower is interpreted Blueprint execution compared to equivalent native C++, and why?
column2: About two orders of magnitude slower, due to instruction dispatch overhead, type tag inspection, stack manipulation, and indirect virtual function calls, versus C++ compiling directly to a few SIMD instructions.

column1: What is Unreal's nativization pipeline and what problem does it solve?
column2: An ahead-of-time compiler that transforms Blueprint bytecode into C++ source code, then compiles it natively—eliminating interpretive overhead to close the ~100x performance gap between Blueprint and native C++.

column1: What are the four invariant principles of Unreal's server-authoritative replication model?
column2: 1) Server owns canonical ground truth via fixed-tick authoritative snapshots, 2) clients run speculative local prediction to mask latency, 3) bandwidth optimization via delta compression and relevancy filtering, 4) RPCs provide explicit imperative network control flow alongside declarative property replication.

column1: How does client-side prediction reconciliation work when a server correction diverges from the local simulation?
column2: The client rewinds its state to the last server-confirmed authoritative frame, then replays all subsequent locally-buffered input commands forward to re-derive a corrected predicted state.

column1: Why does Unreal's replication model favor eventual consistency over strong consistency (unlike Paxos/Raft)?
column2: Real-time games prioritize liveness over safety—a frozen/stuttering experience is worse than transient desync artifacts (rubber-banding, phantom hits), so bounded, rapidly-converging divergence is tolerated instead of blocking consensus.
